body_markdown:
The other day, I had an urge to drive a Studebaker. I looked over at my Lark, still in its disassembled state, and realized that I’m still on the hook for welding in some floor patches. I’m also still waffling on whether it needs a T5 stick-shift transmission swap. That’s going to be a negotiation with my wife, a dyed-in-the-wool automatic driver (but manual tolerator). Given this scenario, my sole remaining Studebaker option was[my 1964 Gran Turismo Hawk](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/against-all-oddities/hawking-for-my-high-school-64-studebaker-part-1/) , the very same that I drove throughout high school.


Thomas, my right-hand man at our ex-foundry-current-car-commune, was the last to drive[the GT Hawk](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/against-all-oddities/hawking-for-my-high-school-studebaker-part-2/) , when he ventured to take it down to Cars and Coffee in Mooresville, North Carolina—about 20 miles away. I recall that he got back closer to dinner time than coffee time… and on the back of a trailer. Shortly after that, we pulled the tank and brought it to our local radiator shop to be boiled for a few days to get all of the rusty junk out of it. No doubt it still held some fraction of the fuel I spent when I was driving this car to my college exams.


Lurking like a Lark.


[Matthew Anderson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/manderson/)


It was safe to assume that, in the 12 months since the fuel incident, other things had deteriorated. But nevertheless, I proceeded. It started alright, at least. But when I went for the brakes at the first stop sign, the steering wheel came spinning out of my hand. *Good morning to you too, nonfunctional brake circuit.* The throttle response was incredibly lazy, which meant I was roasting the “brand-new” clutch—installed in 2003, but hardly used.


Sensing this situation was spiraling before my eyes, I asked my gremlins to get their greasy little paws over[the GT Hawk](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/against-all-oddities/hawking-for-my-high-school-studebaker-part-3/) . I wanted to relive my high school glory days as soon as possible.


We got the Hawk up on the lift, and I started to remember some *other* problems I had conveniently ignored, even as a teen. Looking at the rear leaf spring bushings and shackles reminded me of driving to UNC Wilmington circa 2005. Heading down Highway 40, parked at around 75 miles an hour, the car would abruptly shift three feet to the left or right, seemingly at random. Thomas, from his test drive notes, confirmed that this condition endured. “Any sort of bump or undulation causes the rear end to wag like a dog. Any firm pressure applied to the pedal causes the car to go any direction but straight, usually into oncoming traffic.”


Brilliant. My Studebaker had apparently been equipped with a passive and involuntary rear-steer system via all six leaf spring bushings being no longer present. I have not attempted those speeds since graduation, but it still seems like something we should fix. We figured it might be a good idea to address that while the car was up on the lift.


We also got to digging into the brakes, and I was pleasantly surprised to find that the hoses looked new. I remembered I had installed new brake hoses in my driveway only about three years ago and simply forgotten. *Score!* The right-side wheel cylinder, however, had seized in its bore, creating an involuntary *front* active-steer system as well. Thomas also noted play in the kingpins and idler arm, further involuntary passive chassis control systems we wish to eradicate… eventually. Thankfully, I had over-ordered wheel cylinder repair kits when going through the brakes on the Lark and had an extra on the shelf. Thomas got after it with a hone and the kit and restored symmetrical front braking.


Trying to build brake pressure—the easy way.


[Matthew Anderson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/manderson/)


I suspected the throttle response issue was due to debris being ingested into the needle valve and main jet assemblies, which turned out to be mostly true. Thankfully, I had installed an Edelbrock/Carter AFB replica back in my high school days, which affords us, even today, a high degree of short-notice parts availability.


Thomas’ notes read as such: *“The accelerator pump is a little weak, and the carburetor is due for a cleaning. We had the fuel tank boiled and cleaned out about a year ago. Some trash got pulled up through the system into the carb from then. So full rebuild it is. It also runs a little bit rich, so good time to put a new metering rod and jet set in it. Also, since I have the carburetor out of the way, it’s much easier to get to the distributor now. So I guess I’ll maintenance the points, set the dwell and check the timing. I also have a distributor recurving kit floating around in my toolbox for Delco distributor, why not throw that in as well?* *If I’m rebuilding the carburetor and redoing the distributor, might as well pull the spark plugs out and clean them too?”*


All good things. The fuel pump needs further investigation: Every time I start the car, I have to whack the electric pump with a hammer to get it to cycle. (It’s potentially the source of more debris.) Anyway, that’s a problem for six months from now. On to the next!


Good old Carter AFB… I mean, Edelbrock.


[Matthew Anderson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/manderson/)


Thinking back *again* to that UNC Wilmington trip 20-something years ago, I should also note that I broke down on the way home due to a faulty voltage regulator. Detecting misfires on Highway 40, I made a beeline for S. Saunders St. in Southeast Raleigh and coasted to a halt in a not-so-great neighborhood with wide shoulders. I’m not sure I would do this now, but in my reckless youth, I just walked up to someone’s door, knocked, and asked if they would drive me to an auto parts store. Of course, this was before Google Maps, which would have shown me it was handily walkable. In any case, a nice old man drove me to the parts house and back, and even refused the $10 I offered. I picked up a Group 24 battery (that I needed for my Javelin) and miraculously, the store had the Chrysler voltage regulator I was looking for. I got myself up and running on the side of US-401.


Nine out of 10 breakdowns I suffered in the Hawk during high school and college were directly voltage-regulator related, so I figured that now, nearly 30 years after my initial purchase, it might be time to rectify this issue once and for all. That, and Thomas said he burned his arm on the regulator… *hmm.*


I sat down with pen and paper and drew out the circuits in an attempt to figure out the problem. I got a couple minutes into it and noticed fried traces on the installed regulator unit. Didn’t GM decide this was too much trouble in the ’70s and make an alternator with just one big fat red wire? *One of those, please!* Within an hour, it was cranking out 14.4 volts at idle. Well, that alternator would’ve been a nice li’l nugget to have known about in the Leesville High School parking lot.


Fixed, finally.


[Matthew Anderson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/manderson/)


Regular readers of this column will not be shocked to learn that, soon after this success, I succumbed to my usual reckless and uncontrollable habit of scope creep. While the GT Hawk was up on the lift, I figured it was a good opportunity to see whether the Super T-10 four-speed on the back of my R2 Avanti motor might be the same length as the Borg-Warner three-speed overdrive unit currently installed. Could we be so lucky as to have congruent lengths between the two boxes and a commonized output spline pattern?


No. The universe stopped me.


At this point, we’re not back up and running yet with the Hawk, but we’re close! I’m awaiting a slew of parts from Stephen Allen Studebaker Parts to get the rear axle back together. Maybe, finally, the GT Hawk will ** be better than it was in high school.


See, I do work!


[Matthew Anderson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/manderson/)


Maybe I had done this and forgotten DOT3 soluble grease…
